recall_prompt: Say how you would find this sum — how you rewrite the terms, what you add to both sides and why, which standard form the alternating signs point to, how you find p, q and x, and how you get S back.
insider_note: Alternating signs mean the (1 + x) form, and the missing start is 1 − 1/4, added with its minus sign. The 3/4 comes off again at the end: S = √(2/3) − 3/4.

steps.label: Rewrite with factorials
steps.margin_note: First two marks. Each denominator is a product like 5·10·15 = 5³·(1·2·3), so every term becomes (a product)/(k!) times (1/4)ᵏ. The first term 3/(4·8) is (1·3/2!)(1/4)², so p = 1 and the 1 and the −(1/1!)(1/4) terms are missing: add 1 − 1/4 on both sides. The signs alternate, so compare with the (1 + x) form.
lines: The 1 and the −(1/1!)(1/4) terms are missing,

recall.must_convey: That the series is rewritten so the k-th term is a product over k! times (1/4) to the power k, after adding 1 − 1/4 on both sides so the missing early terms are present.
accept: write each term as a product over k factorial times one by four to the power k and add 1 − 1/4 on both sides
split each denominator into four to the power k times k factorial
add 1 − 1/4 to both sides and bring the series to the shape one plus p by one factorial into x by q and so on
prathi term ni k factorial tho, one by four power k tho rayali, rendu sides ki 1 − 1/4 add cheyali
rewrite the denominators as powers of four times factorials

steps.why: The standard expansion of (1 + x)^(−p/q) has a k! in every denominator and a fixed ratio x/q raised to k. Until the given series is written in that exact shape, p, q and x cannot be read off.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to add 1 − 1/4 on both sides when the series starts late, so the comparison has no 1 to match.
Writing 5·10·15 as 5·3! instead of 5³·3! — every factor carries a 4.
Losing the alternating sign when the terms alternate.

steps.label: Compare with the standard expansion
steps.margin_note: Third mark, for WRITING the standard expansion beside the series. The examiner looks for the pattern p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q) over 1!, 2!, 3!. Alternating signs mean the (1 + x) form.

recall.must_convey: That the series is compared with the expansion of (1 + x) to the power minus p by q, whose coefficients are p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q) over 1!, 2!, 3!.
accept: compare with the expansion of (1 + x) to the power minus p by q
match it with one plus p by one factorial into x by q plus p into p plus q by two factorial into x by q squared and so on
use the standard binomial series with negative fractional index (1 + x) to the power minus p by q
(1 + x)^(−p/q) formula tho compare cheyali
the pattern p then p into p plus q over the factorials is the standard series

steps.why: This is the only binomial expansion whose coefficients grow as p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q). Naming it turns the rest of the question into reading off three numbers.
common_mistakes: Using the (1 − x) form for an alternating series or the (1 + x) form for an all-plus series.
Writing p(p + 1) instead of p(p + q) — the step between factors is q, not 1.

steps.label: Find p, q and x
steps.margin_note: Fourth and fifth marks. p is the first factor (1), p + q is the second (3) so q = 2, and x/q equals the common ratio 1/4 so x = q/4 = 2/4 = 1/2.

recall.must_convey: That p = 1 and p + q = 3 give q = 2, and x/q = 1/4 gives x = one by two.
accept: p is one, p plus q is three so q is two, and x by q is one by four so x is one by two
the first factor gives p equal to one and the second gives q equal to two
x by q equals one by four so x equals one by two
p one, q two vasthai, x by q one by four kabatti x one by two
read off p from the first numerator and q from the gap between the factors

steps.why: Three unknowns need three matches: the first numerator fixes p, the second fixes p + q, and the ratio inside the bracket fixes x/q. Nothing else in the series is free.
common_mistakes: Taking x = 1/4 directly — the bracket holds x/q, so x = q × 1/4.
Reading q from the second factor as a whole instead of as p + q.

steps.label: Evaluate the power
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. Substitute p, q, x into (1 + x)^(−p/q) and simplify the fraction inside the bracket before touching the exponent.

recall.must_convey: That substituting gives three by four plus S equals root of two by three.
accept: substituting gives three by four plus S equals root of two by three
put the values into (1 + x)^(−p/q) and simplify to get three by four plus S equals root of two by three
the bracket becomes three by two and the power gives three by four plus S equals root of two by three
values substitute cheste three by four plus S equals root of two by three vasthundi
simplify the bracket first then apply the negative index
heard_as: three by four plus S equals root of two by three

steps.why: A negative index inverts the fraction and a fractional index takes a root. Doing the inversion first keeps the root over a simple fraction.
common_mistakes: Inverting the exponent instead of the fraction when the index is negative.
Leaving a root in the denominator without a clear final value.

steps.label: Subtract the added terms
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. 1 − 1/4 = 3/4 was added, so it comes off: S = √(2/3) − 3/4.

recall.must_convey: That S is root of two by three minus the added 3/4.

common_mistakes: Using the (1 − x) form and getting √2 instead of √(2/3).
